> Neuroception refers to the brain’s automatic detection of safety or threat without conscious awareness. It is central to Polyvagal Theory and underlies rapid autonomic responses that initiate anxiety before conscious processing occurs (Paulus & Stein, 2010; Harrison et al., 2021). #threat/unconcious_processing #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety #models/polyvagal #perception/neuroception 
> Neuroceptive processes are especially relevant for social trust/distrust judgments—subtle cues can trigger physiological arousal or calmness **even when not consciously perceived** ([[#^782b79|Paulus & Stein, 2010]]). > > The relationship between **anxiety** and **motor control** can be explained through established theoretical frameworks. According to **execution focus models**, anxiety increases **mental effort** and **conscious movement monitoring**, which disrupts automatic control processes (Beilock and Carr, 2001; Nieuwenhuys and Oudejans, 2012). 
> > The constrained action hypothesis further suggests that **anxiety-induced internal focus** impairs the unconscious, reflexive control processes that normally regulate coordinated movement (Wulf et al., 2001). 
> > *These theoretical perspectives suggest that sensorimotor mismatch-induced anxiety can lower automaticity.*

# \#proprioception (2)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> Anxiety manifests biologically through altered somatosensory cortex activity, particularly in the right postcentral gyrus, which directly processes bodily sensations ([[Why Anxiety?#Somatosensory Cortices]], #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety/bio/somatosensory_cortex). The somatosensory cortex participates in emotional regulation and exhibits structural and functional changes in anxiety disorders ([[Target word 'somatosensory_cortex and anxiety or proprioception']], Higher-Order Roles Perception Emotion Social, #cognitive/anxiety/trait_anxiety, #somatosensory_cortex/emotional_regulation). This neural architecture creates a direct pathway through which anxiety disrupts the proprioceptive feedback essential for wearable robot control—proprioception being the sensory modality most affected by wearable robots and carrying the most weight in system performance ([[Why Anxiety?#^9b4e49]], #proprioception). ^tr-4z9f7llbo

# \#cognitive/anxiety/unpredictability (3)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> The definition of robot "performance" is shifting from purely mechanical metrics to human-machine fluency measured by skill-normalized performance and co-adaptation success (Why Anxiety?, The definition of "performance"). Expert performance is reached when the user's visuomotor system has fully "internalized" the robot's physics, measured by movement trajectory stability and decreased visual attention (Why Anxiety?, The definition of "performance"). Visuomotor skill level predicts learning capacity; therefore, robot performance is defined by the speed of the user's "proprioceptive recalibration" and reduction in visual error-correction effort (Why Anxiety?, Claim, #trust_factors/robot_factors/performance). Anxiety sabotages this entire process—during early motor learning, anxious learners cope with high uncertainty by constraining movements into rigid, stereotyped patterns that prevent skill development ([[TagsRoutes/reports/TagReport_#trust_factors__human_factors|TagReport_#trust_factors__human_factors]], #cognitive/anxiety section, #cognitive/anxiety, #motor_control/motor_learning, #trust_factors/robot_factors/uncertainty, #cognitive/anxiety/unpredictability). ^tr-13ru2144k

This high-level belief in unpredictability influences precision weighting across the cortical hierarchy, initially causing prediction-making to become less certain and sensory errors to dominate ([[TagsRoutes/reports/TagReport_#cognitive__anxiety|TagReport_#cognitive__anxiety]], #cognitive/anxiety/unpredictability section). ^tr-6ynjvy4ka

# \#Sensory_Processing/precision (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> Anxiety biases predictive processing, shifting attention and weighting of sensory signals, yielding either rigid or overly variable movements and critically reducing trust in sensory feedback (Target word 'anxiety or threat or safety or risk', [[Anxiety and Proprioception]], Theoretical work, #cognitive/anxiety/predictive_processing_bias, #Sensory_Processing/sensory_integration, #cognitive/anxiety/rigid_movements, #cognitive/anxiety/overly_variable_movements, #cognitive/anxiety/reduced_trust_in_sensory_feedback). In healthy young adults, higher anxiety correlated with greater postural sway and altered reliance on somatosensory and visual input, indicating less efficient sensory integration (Target word 'cognitive or perception', t3, #Sensory_Processing/sensory_integration, #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety, #cognitive/anxiety/greater_sway). High-anxiety patients demonstrated delayed sensory reweighting when proprioception was perturbed, leading to greater postural instability (Target word 'anxiety or threat or safety or risk', [[Anxiety and Proprioception]], t2, #cognitive/anxiety/postural_instability, #Sensory_Processing/precision). ^tr-ojzv6m77q

# \#trust_factors/human_factors/traits/anxiety (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> From evolutionary and psychological perspectives, anxiety functions as a threat-detection system that evolved to keep people vigilant to potential threats, especially social rejection, status loss, or aggression (Target word 'cognitive or perception', What Anxiety Is For Evolutionary Biological, #threat). Early environments shape a generally "threat-sensitive" anxiety system; high baseline anxiety then makes people more wary and less trusting of others (Target word 'anxiety or threat or safety or risk', Direction of Causality, #evolution, #cognitive/anxiety, #threat, #trust_factors/human_factors/traits/anxiety). This creates a vicious cycle: anxiety reduces trust, and reduced trust amplifies anxiety. Meta-analytic evidence confirms that higher attachment anxiety associates with lower interpersonal trust (Why Anxiety?, How Trust and Anxiety Interact Psychologically). Longitudinal data in older adults suggest higher bonding trust predicts lower trait anxiety over time, partly via better self-rated health (Why Anxiety?, Direction of Causality, #trust_factors/human_factors/traits/anxiety). ^tr-6xp9tg9l6

> >M2 selects and sequences the motor programs needed for complex actions. While M1 executes the movement, M2 decides how to perform it. 
> >M2 is located in the [frontal lobe](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/23073-cerebral-cortex), anterior to the [precentral gyrus](https://radiopaedia.org/articles/38614?embed_domain=hackmd.io%252525252f%2525252540yipuafecsl2jsu8smr5njq%252525252fbnjhjgjghjghjghfavicon.ico) (M1). 
> >M2 receives significant input from the [secondary somatosensory cortex (S2)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10350168/). This allows the brain to adjust planned movements based on current sensory feedback (e.g., adjusting your grip on a slippery object). #cognitive/anxiety/state_anxiety/bio/somatosensory_cortex/postcentral_gyrus ^tr-ibrscaq4j

# \#threat (2)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> 
> - Finely tuned motor control breaks down most commonly due to negative emotional state of anxiety. #cognitive/anxiety 
> - What we perceive from the world, is not what it actually is, but the brain's best guess based on a trade-off between the prior probability and the hypothesis that fits the current sensory input. #perception 
> - Our brains select hypotheses in a Bayes-optimal manner, based on how well those hypotheses minimize prediction error. #baysian #prediction_error  ^de0b99
> - In perceptual inference, prediction errors are minimized by the organism updating their model of the world to fit input. #perception/perceptual_inference ^pe
> - In active inference, the prediction is generated and then the (predicted) state of affairs is brought about as part of the prediction error minimisation imperative. #threat #predictive_processing #cognitive/anxiety/hypervigilance  #chemicals/neurotransmitters/Norepinephrine  #neuroscience/active_inrefence_theory ^tr-omd0zzonh

# \#reward_signals (1)
## 1
> [!info]+ 1
> - McDougall [(McDougall, 1936)](https://archive.org/details/introductiontoso00mcdo) proposed a framework that was concerned with “**instincts**”.  
>   Instincts, in our framework, refer to (more or less) evolutionarily hard-wired (i.e., innate) behavior patterns or routines that can be relatively easily triggered by pertinent stimuli in pertinent situations. #cognitive/instincts_model
> - Some of these primary drives are approach-oriented, while others are avoidance-oriented. This distinction has been argued by many (e.g., [(Clark & Watson, 1999)](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1999-04371-012), [(Gray & McNaughton, 2000)](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-neuropsychology-of-anxiety-9780198522713), [(Smillie et al., 2006)](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327957pspr1004_3)).  
>   The approach system is sensitive to cues signaling rewards, and results in active approach.  
>   The avoidance system is sensitive to cues of punishment, and results in avoidance, characterized by **anxiety or fear**. #reward_signals #punishment_cues #cognitive/anxiety #cognitive/fear ^tr-spfecqi79
>
